claims.text: Sec. 1841 carries the note '44 USC 2107 note' and is titled 'UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA RECORDS COLLECTION AT THE NATIONAL ARCHIVES AND RECORDS ADMINISTRATION'. Sec. 1841(a)(1)(A) required the Archivist, within 60 days of enactment, to commence establishment of the 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection'.

Sec. 1841(a)(1)(C) defines the scope of the Collection: 'record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects), which shall be transmitted to the National Archives in accordance with section 2107 of title 44, United States Code.' The phrases 'technologies of unknown origin' and 'non-human intelligence' are enacted federal statutory text.

Sec. 1842(a)(2) imposes absolute prohibitions: '(A) Destruction; alteration; mutilation.--No unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be destroyed, altered, or mutilated in any way. (B) ... No unidentified anomalous phenomena record made available or disclosed to the public prior to the date of the enactment of this Act may be withheld, redacted, postponed for public disclosure, or reclassified. (C) ... No unidentified anomalous phenomena record created by a person or entity outside the Federal Government ... shall be withheld, redacted, postponed for public disclosure, or reclassified.'

Sec. 1842(c)(1) required each head of a Government office, not later than 300 days after enactment (i.e. by approximately 16 October 2024), to 'review, identify, and organize each unidentified anomalous phenomena record in the custody or possession of the office for (A) disclosure to the public; and (B) transmission to the Archivist.'

Sec. 1843(a) sets the postponement standard: disclosure 'may be postponed ... if the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' of one of four harms, including that public disclosure would reveal 'any other matter currently relating to the military defense, intelligence operations, or conduct of foreign relations of the United States, the disclosure of which would demonstrably and substantially impair the national security of the United States'. The determination is made by the agency holding the record; no independent board reviews it.

Sec. 1842(g)(2)(D) sets the outer disclosure deadline: 'Each unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be publicly disclosed in full, and available in the Collection, not later than the date that is 25 years after the date of the first creation of the record by the originating body, unless the President certifies that-- (i) continued postponement is made necessary by an identifiable harm to the military defense, intelligence operations, law enforcement, or conduct of foreign relations; and (ii) the identifiable harm is of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure.'

Sec. 1843(b) allows unilateral withdrawal: 'Senior Agency Officials designated in accordance with Executive Order 13526 or any successor Orders may withdraw records in the Collection that are determined to be both not related to unidentified anomalous phenomena and properly classified', subject only to notification of congressional leadership and the oversight committees named in sec. 1841(e).

Sec. 1841(e) assigns continuing legislative oversight of the Collection to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Armed Services, and Select Intelligence Committees, and to the House Oversight and Accountability, Armed Services, and Permanent Select Intelligence Committees.

claims.source: PL 118-31 Div. A, Title XVIII, Subtitle C, table of contents and full text
claims.text: Subtitle C as enacted consists of only three sections: 1841 (Records Collection at NARA), 1842 (review, identification, transmission, public disclosure by Government offices), and 1843 (grounds for postponement). The enacted text contains no 'Review Board' and no 'eminent domain' language.

Division G (Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024), sec. 7343(b): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this division may be obligated or expended in support of any activity involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation unless the Director of National Intelligence has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate committees of Congress and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.'

Sec. 7343(c): 'Independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available to the appropriate congressional committees and leadership.' This is a defense-contractor IR&D cost-allowability lever aimed at privately funded UAP work.
Sec. 7341 amends 50 U.S.C. 3373(k)(1) to shift the annual UAP report obligation from the DNI and SecDef jointly to 'the Director of the Office' (AARO).
PL 118-31 was 'Approved December 22, 2023.'

Sec. 7343(b)'s funding cutoff is drafted as a conditional, not a prohibition: IC money may be spent on UAP special-access activity IF the DNI briefs Congress. The provision therefore concedes, in enacted law, that such special-access UAP activity may be under way and that Congress had not been told about it. Reasoning: a limitation clause presupposes the existence of the class of activity it limits, and the phrase 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation' has no other referent.

desc: P.L. 118-31 is the document that records the stripping. The Senate passed S. 2226 on 27 July 2023 carrying two separate UAP regimes: Division G, the fifteen-section UAP Disclosure Act, and Division M Section 1102, Warner's contractor turn-in inside the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024. The Act signed on 22 December 2023 contains, in place of Division G, a three-section Subtitle C of Title XVIII: Sec. 1841, the Records Collection at the National Archives; Sec. 1842, review and transmission by heads of Government offices within 300 days; and Sec. 1843, grounds for postponement. There is no Sec. 9007 equivalent, no Sec. 9010 equivalent, no Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan and no authorization of appropriations. In place of Sec. 1102 it contains Sec. 7343, a bare funding limitation. The Act does retain teeth in two places the House committees controlled: Sec. 1687 cuts off DoD funds for UAP activity 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations' unless the Secretary of Defense has described it to the defence and intelligence committees and congressional leadership, and bars independent research and development funding on UAP from being charged as an indirect expense unless disclosed. Sec. 7343 does the same on the intelligence side. Both are one-year limitations tied to funds authorised by that Act, and neither was renewed in FY2025 or FY2026.

claims.text: Section 1687(a) of P.L. 118-31 provides: "None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024."

Section 1687(b) provides that, consistent with DoD Instruction 3204.01 (August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2 dated July 9, 2020), "independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership."

Section 1687(c) defines "appropriate congressional committees" as the congressional defense committees plus HPSCI and SSCI, and "congressional leadership" as the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House.

Section 1841(a)(1)(C) provides that the Collection "shall consist of record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects)."

Section 1842(c)(1) required each head of a Government office to review, identify and organize each UAP record in its custody within 300 days of enactment; NARA implemented this as a deadline of October 20, 2024, and stated it would accept only digital versions.

Section 1842(g)(2)(D) requires each UAP record to be publicly disclosed in full not later than 25 years after its first creation "unless the President certifies that (i) continued postponement is made necessary by an identifiable harm to the military defense, intelligence operations, law enforcement, or conduct of foreign relations; and (ii) the identifiable harm is of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure."

Section 1843(a) vests the postponement determination in "the original classification authority" on a finding of "clear and convincing evidence" of one of four enumerated harms — restoring the decision to the classifying agency rather than the independent board the Senate had proposed; section 1843(b) permits Senior Agency Officials to withdraw records from the Collection determined to be both unrelated to UAP and properly classified on 60 days' advance notice to congressional leadership and the oversight committees, and section 1843(c) requires notice of any postponement within 15 days.

Section 7343 imposes a parallel funding cutoff on Intelligence Authorization funds, substituting the Director of National Intelligence for the Secretary of Defense and adding the Appropriations Committees to the notification list; its subsection (c) contains a dangling reference to "contracts covered by such instruction" with no instruction identified anywhere in that section.

The chairmen of the House and Senate intelligence committees entered an Explanatory Statement in the Congressional Record of December 14, 2023 stating that section 7343 "is also intended to avoid technology and security stovepipes and expand awareness regarding any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes if they are shown to exist."

Now it means that declassification of UAP records will be largely up to the same entities that blocked and obfuscated their disclosure for decades," and in the same colloquy: "We have also been notified by multiple credible sources that information on UAPs has also been withheld from Congress, which, if true, is a violation of the laws requiring full notification to the legislative branch, especially as it relates to the four congressional leaders, Defense Committees, and the Intelligence Committee."

connections: P.L. 118-31 secs. 1841-1843 are the surviving remnant of S.Amdt. 797, the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act; the deletions are itemized in the Joint Explanatory Statement at p. 1330.

Section 1687 aims directly at the waived and unacknowledged SAP mechanism of 10 U.S.C. 119 and DoDI 5205.11 by conditioning appropriations on disclosure to the defense and intelligence committees and the four leaders.
Section 1687(b) and section 7343(c) target contractor independent research and development indirect expense under DoDI 3204.01 — the funding path that bypasses DoD program elements entirely.
The 300-day review obligation runs against every 'Government office,' expressly including the NRO, CIA, DOE and the military departments; NARA set the compliance date at October 20, 2024.

AARO is written into the statute at sec. 1842(c)(2)(E)-(F) and sec. 1842(c)(3) as a recipient of agency records, after conferees removed the Senate requirement that SAPs provide UAP material to AARO under sec. 1687.
Sean Kirkpatrick and OUSD(I&S) are the named actors whose November 2023 redline shaped the conference outcome.
Sec. 7341 shifted the annual UAP report obligation from the Secretary of Defense and the DNI to AARO and its director.
dossier.denialPosture: The Presidential signing statement of December 22, 2023 is the operative denial artifact: it identified section 1687 as one of several provisions compelling delivery of highly sensitive classified information to Congress and reserved to the Executive a construction of those provisions consistent with its own view of national security — a reservation aimed squarely at the one UAP provision with a funding sanction attached.
dossier.narrative:
The FY2024 NDAA is a 973-page enrolled bill authorizing $886 billion. The Senate approved the conference version 87-13 on 13 December 2023, the House 310-118 the next day, and the President signed it on 22 December.

Section 1687, "Limitation on Use of Funds for Certain Unreported Programs," is the money clause. Subsection (a): "None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024." Subsection (b) closes the contractor channel: citing DoD Instruction 3204.01, it provides that independent research and development funding relating to UAP "shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership." The missing preposition is in the enacted text. Subsection (c) defines the appropriate committees as the congressional defense committees plus HPSCI and SSCI, and congressional leadership as the four leaders.

That IR&D subsection is the sleeper. It is a legislative acknowledgment that UAP-related work might sit inside contractor overhead accounts rather than a government program element — funded by the government as an allowable indirect cost without ever appearing as a DoD program. Congress does not write a prohibition against a billing practice nobody uses.

The Joint Explanatory Statement explains what the conferees did to the Senate provision (formerly section 1646): they removed the direction to provide information to AARO, and summarized the prohibition. Then they wrote six numbered categories of activity the prohibition "could cover": recruiting, employing, equipping and providing security for government or contractor personnel with a mission of "capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft"; analyzing such craft or components "including for the purpose of determining properties, material composition, method of manufacture, origin, characteristics, usage and application, performance, operational modalities, or reverse engineering of such craft or component technology"; protecting UAP activities and information "from disclosure or compromise"; actions relating to reverse engineering or replicating UAP technology or performance; development of propulsion technology or aerospace craft "based on or derived from or inspired by" reverse engineering of recovered UAP craft or materials; and "Any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust." That sixth category is a definition by exclusion of every propulsion method the conferees could not name.

Section 7343 does the same on the Intelligence Authorization side, substituting the DNI for the Secretary of Defense and adding the Appropriations Committees. Its IR&D subsection contains a dangling cross-reference — "contracts covered by such instruction," with no instruction identified anywhere in the section. The intelligence committee chairmen entered an Explanatory Statement in the Congressional Record on 14 December 2023 saying section 7343 was intended "to avoid technology and security stovepipes and expand awareness regarding any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes if they are shown to exist."

Sections 1841-1843 are the records regime. Section 1841 directs the Archivist, within 60 days of enactment, to commence establishing the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection," consisting of "record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects)." Those three terms appear in enacted United States statute with no definitions attached, because the definitions lived in the Senate bill and were dropped. Congress legislated about non-human intelligence and then declined to say what it meant.

Section 1842 sets the mechanics. Each head of a government office had 300 days to review, identify and organize its UAP records; NARA fixed the operative date at 20 October 2024. No UAP record may be destroyed, altered or mutilated, and no record already publicly disclosed may be withheld, redacted, postponed or reclassified. Agencies must give precedence to records "that most unambiguously and definitively pertain to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence," to records under active FOIA litigation, and to records "with earliest provenance." Subsection (g)(2)(D) is the 25-year rule: each record must be disclosed in full not later than 25 years after creation unless the President certifies continued postponement is necessary because of "an identifiable harm to the military defense, intelligence operations, law enforcement, or conduct of foreign relations" of "such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure."

Section 1843 is where the Senate's design was inverted. Postponement is decided not by an independent board but by "the original classification authority," on "clear and convincing evidence" of one of four enumerated harms.

The JES at page 1330 states the outcome without euphemism: "The agreement does not include the provisions that would establish an independent Review Board, a Review Board staff, eminent domain authority, or a controlled disclosure process."

On 13 December 2023 Schumer told the Senate: "It is really an outrage that the House didn't work with us on adopting our proposal for a review board... Now it means that declassification of UAP records will be largely up to the same entities that blocked and obfuscated their disclosure for decades." He added that multiple credible sources had notified them that UAP information was being withheld from Congress, "which, if true, is a violation of the laws requiring full notification to the legislative branch." Nine days later the President signed the bill and issued a signing statement listing section 1687 among provisions requiring submission of "highly sensitive classified information" to Congress.
openQuestions: Whether any agency has ever certified compliance with section 1687, and whether any funds have been withheld or an activity terminated under it.

Which agencies transmitted records to the UAP Records Collection by the October 20, 2024 deadline, in what volume, and how many records were postponed under section 1843 and reported under the 15-day notice rule.
How many records have been withdrawn from the Collection under section 1843(b) by Senior Agency Officials, and on what basis.
Whether the President has ever made a section 1842(g)(2)(D) certification to continue postponing a UAP record beyond 25 years.

How agencies are interpreting the undefined statutory terms 'technologies of unknown origin,' 'non-human intelligence' and 'temporarily non-attributed objects' in their identification and review, and whether NARA issued any definitional guidance beyond the metadata template.

Whether any contractor has been denied recovery of independent research and development indirect costs under section 1687(b) or section 7343(c), which would be a Defense Contract Audit Agency and Defense Contract Management Agency record.
Who the 'multiple credible sources' were who told Schumer information had been withheld from Congress.
dossier.whatItIs: The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, H.R. 2670, became Public Law 118-31 on December 22, 2023. It contains four UAP-related provisions: section 1687 (funding cutoff for unreported UAP special access programs), sections 1841-1843 (the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the National Archives), section 7341 (a reporting-channel adjustment) and section 7343 (the parallel Intelligence Authorization funding cutoff). It is what survived of the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act after House-Senate conference.
dossier.whyImplicated: The enacted law is simultaneously the strongest and the weakest document on this board. Strongest, because the Joint Explanatory Statement of the House-Senate conference committee states in the official legislative history that the section 1687 funding prohibition "could cover" activities including "Analyzing such craft, or pieces or components thereof," "Actions relating to reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology or performance," propulsion "based on or derived from or inspired by inspection, analysis, or reverse engineering of recovered unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or materials," and "Any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust." Conferees do not write six itemized categories of a thing that does not exist. Weakest, because everything with teeth was removed: the same JES records that "The agreement does not include the provisions that would establish an independent Review Board, a Review Board staff, eminent domain authority, or a controlled disclosure process," and section 1843 hands the postponement decision back to "the original classification authority" — the same officials the Senate bill was designed to review. The difference between the Senate text and the enacted text is the measurable output of the concealment effort in a single legislative cycle.

timeline.label: The stripping is enacted
timeline.text: P.L. 118-31 is signed. Fifteen sections become three. The Review Board, the eminent domain clause, the Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan, the $20,000,000 authorization, the contractor turn-in and the immunity grant are all gone. Sec. 7343 is left referring to an instruction it no longer identifies.

timeline.label: Eminent domain and the contractor inventory are stripped; the IR&D clause survives
timeline.text: Public Law 118-31 is enacted without the Review Board, the eminent domain provision or the SSCI contractor disclosure regime. It retains the records collection at Secs. 1841-1843 and the funding limitations at Secs. 1687 and 7343, including the IR&D restriction citing DoDI 3204.01 by change date.

timeline.label: FY2024 NDAA creates the UAP Records Collection
timeline.text: Sections 1841-1843 of P.L. 118-31 mandate a UAP Records Collection at the National Archives - without the review board, subpoena power or contractor reach in the original UAP Disclosure Act.

timeline.label: FY2024 NDAA enacted with the Review Board and eminent domain stripped
timeline.text: Public Law 118-31 is approved. Only secs. 9004-9006 of the Senate's Division G survive, renumbered as secs. 1841-1843 in Division A, Title XVIII, Subtitle C. The enacted text contains no Review Board and no eminent-domain provision. Postponement decisions revert to 'the original classification authority' holding the record, and Senior Agency Officials may unilaterally withdraw records from the Collection on notice to Congress. Sec. 1687 and IAA sec. 7343 impose conditional funding limits on unreported UAP special-access activity.
